title: Gideon and the Bell
premise: Juniper Vane takes a routine appraisal of Hollowmere House, a derelict property whose valuation figures shift on their own and whose doors refuse to stay counted. When his overnight sleep-recorder captures a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud, Juniper learns the house was built over a drowned chapel whose bell was stolen in 1974 by the surveyor who vanished mid-appraisal. The voice belongs to Edith Marsh, the vanished man's partner, bound to the frost patterns that creep across the windows each night. To survive the winter solstice, when the frost completes its final pattern and claims the house's occupant, Juniper must find the bell, return it to the flooded chapel, and choose between keeping Edith's secret—which would free her but damn the next surveyor—or telling the truth, which frees them both at the cost of everything Juniper has convinced himself he is.
about_author: Tamsin Galloway is a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties before turning to fiction. She writes horror about houses that remember, drawing on the paperwork, folklore, and quiet dread of her surveying years.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: Juniper Vane arrives at Hollowmere House for a court-ordered appraisal, noting its impossible measurements—rooms larger inside than out. His POV establishes his ritual: lights on, doors counted, recorder running. The emotional beat is controlled unease; he treats dread like a line item. A neighbor warns him the last surveyor never left.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Themselves
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. He counts eleven doors at dusk; at midnight there are twelve, and the new one is warm. The appraisal figures in his report change overnight without his hand touching them. Emotional beat: professional denial cracking—he blames drafts, settling foundations, anything but intent.

chapters.title: Frost in July
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Frost ferns bloom across the interior windows despite summer heat, forming patterns too regular to be natural. He photographs them; the photos develop differently each time he views them. Emotional beat: the first admission that the house is watching him back.

chapters.title: The Recorder's Second Voice
chapters.summary: Juniper plays back his sleep recording and hears a woman's voice answering questions in his own pauses—questions he never asked aloud. Her answers are patient, almost kind. Emotional beat: terror braided with loneliness; someone in this house wants to talk to him.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: Juniper speaks into the recorder deliberately, and the voice—Edith Marsh—answers directly. She says she has been here since 1974, since the bell was taken. She asks him to leave while he still can. Emotional beat: reluctant intimacy; she is protecting him, which means something here needs protecting from.

chapters.title: The 1974 File
chapters.summary: Juniper researches the county archive: surveyor Aldous Crane vanished mid-appraisal in 1974; his partner Edith Marsh was declared dead the same winter, though no body surfaced. The stolen item listed as 'recovered' is a chapel bell. Emotional beat: the past is not past—it is load-bearing.

chapters.title: What the House Appraises
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. He realizes the shifting valuations aren't random—the house appraises memories, pricing what he'd pay to keep or lose them. It offers him numbers for his mother's death, his failed marriage. Emotional beat: seduction; survival here means selling pieces of yourself.

chapters.title: The Drowned Chapel
chapters.summary: Juniper finds the flooded chapel on the property's old plat maps, submerged when the reservoir went in decades ago. Edith confirms through the recorder: the bell belongs in its tower, and the frost pattern is a map to it. Emotional beat: purpose replacing fear.

chapters.title: Crane's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the sealed twelfth room, Juniper finds Aldous Crane's survey ledger, its final entries written in a hand deteriorating into frost-script. Crane took the bell to sell it; the house took him instead. Emotional beat: recognition—Crane made every choice Juniper is being offered.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: Edith tells Juniper the truth: she helped Crane steal the bell to escape their debts, and the house has held her ever since as collateral. Freeing her requires returning the bell—but also someone willing to speak the truth of 1974 aloud in the chapel. Emotional beat: guilt as architecture.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The house makes Juniper an offer through the appraisal sheets: sign off on a false valuation, walk away rich, and forget Edith. The frost patterns begin spelling his own name. Emotional beat: temptation sharpened by deadline—the solstice approaches.

chapters.title: Loyalty to a Voice
chapters.summary: Juniper realizes he loves Edith—not romantically at first, but as the only honest presence in a dishonest place. He refuses the offer and burns the false valuation. The house retaliates: doors vanish, lights fail, the cold moves in. Emotional beat: commitment with consequences.

chapters.title: Winter Comes Early
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The reservoir freezes unnaturally fast; the frost pattern nears completion. He can see the chapel tower's tip beneath the ice. Edith warns him the final pattern will claim whoever occupies the house at solstice—him, unless the bell rings first. Emotional beat: countdown dread.

chapters.title: The Weight of Bronze
chapters.summary: Juniper locates the bell in a county storage annex, mislabeled as scrap since 1975. Moving it costs him nearly everything—his truck dies, his savings drain through impossible fees, his employer threatens termination. Emotional beat: the price of doing right compounds daily.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Edith confesses the deeper theft: Crane didn't act alone, and Juniper learns the house itself was once a living thing—a chapel community—that the bell's removal killed. Returning it isn't restitution to a haunting; it's resurrection. Emotional beat: moral stakes clarified.

chapters.title: The Employer's Visit
chapters.summary: Juniper's supervisor arrives demanding the completed appraisal, revealing the firm has known about Hollowmere for fifty years and profited from every vanished surveyor's fees. He offers Juniper Crane's old partnership. Emotional beat: institutional evil; the system wants him complicit.

chapters.title: Breaking the Ice
chapters.summary: On the eve of solstice, Juniper hauls the bell across the frozen reservoir toward the chapel tower, frost writing its final spirals behind him. The ice groans, opens, tries to take the bell back down. Emotional beat: physical ordeal mirroring spiritual choice.

chapters.title: The Truth Spoken
chapters.summary: Inside the drowned chapel's air pocket, Juniper hangs the bell and speaks the truth of 1974 aloud—Crane's theft, Edith's complicity, the firm's cover-up. The bell swings once without being touched. Emotional beat: confession as key; truth as mechanism.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings
chapters.summary: Climax. The bell tolls through water and stone; the frost pattern completes and then unravels. The house exhales fifty years of held breath. Edith appears to Juniper whole and warm for one moment before the choice: the truth frees her, but the house demands a keeper. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Keeper
chapters.summary: Juniper understands the final term: someone must remain as the house's honest witness, or the cycle begins again with the next surveyor. Edith refuses to let him stay; he refuses to let the pattern restart. They bargain with the house together—the first occupants ever to negotiate rather than be taken. Emotional beat: love against duty, both refusing the script.

chapters.title: A Fair Valuation
chapters.summary: Resolution begins. Juniper files the truest appraisal of his career: Hollowmere House, valued at exactly what was lost in 1974 and what was returned. The county accepts it without question. The twelfth door closes forever; eleven remain, all accounted for. Emotional beat: quiet restoration.

chapters.title: Lights On
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Juniper's POV. He keeps the house—not as prisoner but as steward—and Edith remains, alive again in the way the house allows, tending the chapel bell. On winter nights they count the doors together and the frost draws only ordinary ferns. Emotional beat: earned peace; survival that cost everything except what mattered.
